adjourn.e: From Middle English ajournen, from Old French ajorner (French ajourner), from the phrase a jor (nomé) ("to an (appointed) day").

d.g: To declare to be.
To deem or determine to be.
To award judicially; to assign.
To sentence; to condemn.
d.x: on failure of payment of the fines adjudged against them […] for which he shall be so adjudged to imprisonment

adjudge.e: From Middle English ajugen, adjugen, from Old French ajugier, from Latin adiudicare. Doublet of adjudicate.

d.g: To decide, rule on, or settle as a judge.
d.x: In North Carolina, provisional ballots are adjudicated to determine whether the voter was eligible to cast the ballot.

d.g: To act as a judge.
To seize or convey as security.

adjudicate.e: Borrowed from Latin adiūdicō, adiūdicātus, from ad + iūdicō (“to judge”). Doublet of adjudge.

d.g: To issue a formal command.
To earnestly appeal to or advise; to charge solemnly.
d.x: Party members are adjured to promote awareness of this problem.

adjure.e: From Middle English adjuren, from Latin adiūrō (“beg earnestly”), from ad- (“near, at; towards, to”)' + iūrō (“swear by oath”).

d.g: To modify.
d.x: Morimoto's recipes are adjusted to suit the American palate.

d.g: To improve or rectify.
d.x: He adjusted his initial conclusion to reflect the new data.

d.g: To settle an insurance claim.
To change to fit circumstances.
d.x: Most immigrants adjust quickly to a new community.

adjust.e: From Middle English ajusten, borrowed from Middle French adjuster, or Old French, from Latin ad (“to, up to, towards”) + iustus (“correct, proper, exact”); Equivalent to ad- + just. Probably influenced in sense by Old French ajouster (cf. modern ajouter), from Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre, from Latin iuxta. …

d.g: To measure.
To survey and lay off a due portion to, as of dower in real estate or of pasture held in common.

admeasure.e: From Middle English amesure, from Anglo-Norman amesurer, admesurer, from Medieval Latin admēnsūrō. Compare Classical Latin admētior (“measure out to”).

d.g: To apportion out, distribute.
d.x: [Let zephyrs] administer their tepid, genial airs.

d.g: To manage or supervise the conduct, performance or execution of; to govern or regulate the parameters for the conduct, performance or execution of; to work in an administrative capacity.
d.x: For forms of government let fools contest: / Whate'er is best administered is best.

d.g: To minister (to).
d.x: administering to the sick

d.g: To settle, as the estate of one who dies without a will, or whose will fails of an executor.

administer.e: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

d.g: to administer
the act or function of providing maintenance and general housekeeping for computer systems, networks, peripheral equipment, etc.
d.x: The job is to administrate the network.

administrate.e: * archaic: Latin administrātus, past participle of administrō. * modern: Back-formation from administration (from Latin administrātiō, also from administrō) (The exact etymology is disputed, see note below.)

d.g: To regard with wonder and delight.
To look upon with an elevated feeling of pleasure, as something which calls out approbation, esteem, love or reverence.
To estimate or value highly; to hold in high esteem.
d.x: to admire a person of high moral worth

d.g: To be enthusiastic about (doing something); to want or like (to do something). (Sometimes followed by to.)
d.x: I'm not sayin' she's touched the Devil, now, but I'd admire to know what books she reads and why she hides them — she'll not answer me, y' see.

admire.e: From Middle English admyren, borrowed from Middle French admirer, from Latin admīror, from ad + mīror (“wonder at”).

d.g: To allow to enter; to grant entrance (to), whether into a place, into the mind, or into consideration
d.x: to admit a serious thought into the mind

d.g: To allow (someone) to enter a profession or to enjoy a privilege; to recognize as qualified for a franchise.
d.x: to admit an attorney to practice law

d.g: To concede as true; to acknowledge or assent to, as an allegation which it is impossible to deny (+ to).
d.x: the argument or fact is admitted

d.g: To be capable of; to permit. In this sense, "of" may be used after the verb, or may be omitted.
d.x: The words do not admit such a construction.

admit.e: From Middle English admitten, amitten, borrowed from Old French admettre, amettre (“to admit”), from Latin admittō (“to allow entrance, inlet”, literally “to send to”), from ad- + mittere (“to send”).

d.g: To mingle with something else; to mix.
d.x: Therefore in our account of the development of their intellectual ideas, we also admix pertinent personal details.

d.g: The act of admixing.
d.x: In light (vision) the admix results in white and in pigments the admix results in grey.

d.g: The mixture that results from admixing, especially an alloy.
d.x: In the late 1990s metal-reinforced glass ionomers were introduced for use as core buildups. These contain a silver alloy admix.

admix.e: Back-formation from admixture; analyzable as ad- + mix.

d.g: To inform or notify of a fault; to rebuke in a serious tone; to tell off.
d.x: Better is a poore and a wise child, then an old and foolish king who will no more be admonished.

d.g: To advise against wrongdoing; to caution; to warn against danger or an offense.
To instruct or direct.

admonish.e: Inherited from Middle English a(d)monisshen (adapted through -ishen (“-ish”) from earlier amonesten), from Old French amonester (modern French admonester), from an unattested Late Latin or Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, from Latin admoneō (“to remind, warn”), from ad- + moneō (“to warn, advise”).

d.g: to become adolescent; to pass through adolescence.
d.x: The children are beginning to adolesce around the age of 12.

adolesce.e: Back-formation from adolescence. First attested in 1859.

d.g: To take voluntarily (a child of other parents) to be in the place of, or as, one's own child.
d.x: A friend of mine recently adopted a Chinese baby girl found on the streets of Beijing.

d.g: To obtain (a pet) from a shelter or the wild.
d.x: We're going to adopt a Dalmatian.

d.g: To contribute towards the upkeep of (a child or animal), in exchange for occasional stories, pictures, etc.
d.x: We adopted an elephant at the local zoo.

d.g: To take by choice into the scope of one's responsibility.
d.x: This supermarket chain adopts several families every Yuletide, providing them with money and groceries for the holidays.

adopt.e: From Middle French adopter, from Latin adoptō; ad + optō (“to choose, desire”), equivalent to ad- + opt.

d.g: To worship.
d.x: Now, gods that we adore, whereof comes this?

d.g: To love with one's entire heart and soul; regard with deep respect and affection.
d.x: It is obvious to everyone that Gerry adores Heather.

d.g: To be very fond of.

adore.e: From Middle English *adoren, aouren, from Old French adorer, aorer, from Latin adōrō (“to pray to”), from ad (“to”) + ōrō (“to speak”).

d.g: To make more beautiful and attractive; to decorate.
d.x: a man adorned with noble statuary and columns

adorn.e: From Middle English adornen, adournen, from Latin adōrnāre; from ad- + ōrnō (“furnish, embellish”). See adore, ornate. Replaced earlier Middle English aournen (“to adorn”) borrowed from Old French aorner, from the same Latin source.

d.g: To accumulate on a surface, by adsorption.
d.x: The gas was purified by adsorbing the impurities onto active carbon.

adsorb.e: From French adsorber, from Latin ad- (“to”) + sorbeō (“suck in”).

d.g: To flatter effusively.

adulate.e: A learned borrowing from Latin adūlor.

d.g: To foreshadow vaguely.
To give a vague outline.
To obscure or overshadow.

adumbrate.e: Borrowed from Latin adumbrātus (“represented in outline”), from adumbrāre (“cast a shadow on”), from umbra (“shadow”).

d.g: To transport (something) by advection.
To give (especially public) notice of (something); to announce publicly.
To provide information about a person or goods and services to influence others.
d.x: For personal needs, advertise on the internet or in a local newspaper.

d.g: To provide public information about (a product, service etc.) in order to attract public awareness and increase sales.
d.x: Over the air, they advertise their product on drive-time radio talk shows and TV news shows.

d.g: In gin rummy, to discard a card of one's preferred suit so as to mislead the opponent into thinking you do not want it.

advertise.e: From Middle English advertisen, from Anglo-Norman advertir (“to inform”), avertir, Middle French advertir, avertir (“to warn, give notice to”), with the French -iss- infix assimilated to -ise, -ize and probably influenced by the noun advertisement. Compare also advert.

d.g: Alternative spelling of advertise.

advertize.e: Modelled on advertise, with the -ize suffix.

d.g: To give advice to; to offer an opinion to, as worthy or expedient to be followed.
d.x: The dentist advised me to brush three times a day.

d.g: To recommend; to offer as advice.
d.x: The dentist advised brushing three times a day.

d.g: To formally give information or notice to; to inform or counsel.
d.x: We were advised of the risk.

d.g: To consider, to deliberate.
d.x: […] Samson is reported to the King accordingly. His Majesty, advising of it for a moment, orders that Samson be brought in with the other Twelve.
